description.value: The study assessed fMRI responses to food, cocaine, and neutral cues presented subliminally and supraliminally, and examined diurnal variability in cue reactivity.

spans.text: Here we assessed functional MRI (fMRI) responses to food, cocaine, and neutral cues presented at a subliminal ("unconscious", 33 ms) and supraliminal ("conscious", 750 and 3000 ms) level in healthy, cocaine naïve volunteers.

Additionally, because there is evidence of circadian variability in reward sensitivity (Byrne et al. 2017; Webb et al. 2009), we also aimed to assess if the reactivity to food and drug cues show diurnal variation for which we compared cue-induced brain activation in the morning versus evening.

design.value: Sixteen healthy volunteers completed repeated fMRI sessions with food, cocaine, and neutral cues presented in randomized order at 33, 750, and 3000 ms, with testing once in the morning and once in the evening.

spans.text: Sixteen healthy volunteers underwent 3 fMRI sessions in which 40 cocaine cues, 40 food cues (20 high-caloric foods, 20 low-caloric foods), and 40 neutral cues were presented in randomized order.
Each participant performed the 3 sessions twice on 2 separate days, once between 9 and 11 AM and once between 5 and 7 PM, in randomized order.
Neutral pictures included neutral items from the International Affective Picture System (IAPS) (Lang et al. 2008) and from in-house pictures libraries (Childress et al. 2008; Volkow et al. 2006).

task_description.value: A randomized event-related visual cue task presenting food, cocaine-related, and neutral images at 33, 750, or 3000 ms, repeated in morning and evening sessions.

spans.text: A total of 40 appetitive food, 40 cocaine-related and 40 neutral images were presented in a randomized order in an event-related design using E-prime software.

stimuli.value: Appetitive high- and low-calorie food images, cocaine-related images, and neutral images.

spans.text: Food pictures included appetitive high and low calorie foods, both savory and sweet, both breakfast and dinner items (i.e., bagels, sandwiches, ice cream and sorbet, salads, fruit salad, pizza, hamburgers, pies). Cocaine pictures included bags of cocaine, lines of cocaine on a table, cocaine in spoons, cocaine pipes, and people smoking cocaine (with faces cut off). Neutral pictures included neutral items from the International Affective Picture System (IAPS) (Lang et al. 2008) and from in-house pictures libraries (Childress et al. 2008; Volkow et al. 2006).
